{{Short description|Side of a right triangle}}
{{about|the geometric meaning|the insect|Cathetus (moth)|the plant|Phyllanthus}}

[[Image:Triangle Sides.svg|frame|A right-angled triangle where ''c''<sub>1</sub> and ''c''<sub>2</sub> are the catheti and ''h'' is the hypotenuse]]

In a [[right triangle]], a '''cathetus''' (originally from [[Greek language|Greek]] {{lang|el|κάθετος}}, "perpendicular"; plural: '''catheti'''), commonly known as a '''leg''', is either of the sides that are adjacent to the [[right angle]]. It is occasionally called a "side about the right angle". The side opposite the right angle is the [[hypotenuse]]. In the context of the hypotenuse, the catheti are sometimes referred to simply as "the other two sides".

If the catheti of a right triangle have equal lengths, the triangle is [[isosceles]]. If they have different lengths, a distinction can be made between the minor (shorter) and major (longer) cathetus. The [[ratio]] of the lengths of the catheti defines the [[trigonometric functions]] tangent and cotangent <!-- PLEASE DO NOT link [[tangent]] (that article is about a tangent line) or [[cotangent]] (that redirects to [[Trigonometric functions]] --> of the [[acute angle]]s in the triangle: the ratio <math>c_1/c_2</math>  is the tangent of the acute angle adjacent to <math>c_2</math> and is also the cotangent of the acute angle adjacent to <math>c_1</math>.

In a right triangle, the length of a cathetus is the [[geometric mean]] of the length of the adjacent segment cut by the [[altitude (geometry)|altitude]] to the hypotenuse and the length of the whole hypotenuse.

By the [[Pythagorean theorem]], the sum of the squares of the lengths of the catheti is equal to the square of the length of the hypotenuse.

In architecture, the term '''cathetus''' has been used for the eye of the [[volute]]. It was so termed because its position is determined, in an [[Ionic order|Ionic]] (or voluted) [[capital (architecture)|capital]], by a line let down from the point in which the volute generates.<ref>{{EB1911|inline=y|wstitle=Cathetus|volume=5|page=532}}</ref>
